source.title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems

accepted.question_text: Does a distinct kind of representational time come into being with the origin or development of life, where living systems have representations of past and future states that enable memory, prediction, anticipation, learning, and action beyond immediate reaction in natural time?
accepted.context_brief: representational time and origin of life

evidence.quote:
Here, in contrast, we take a representational stance, and say that past and future exist as properties
of another kind of time, which we call representational time [33]. This representational time appears
along with the origin of life, as a necessary property of living systems 4. We stress that, despite its name,
representational time is not simply a representation of natural time: it is a new kind of time, one that
permits a view of the world that transcends what is possible with natural time, permitting agents to
form memories of the past, make predictions of possible futures, and act on these , rather than merely
react to the immediate.

Is there a new concept of time that comes into being with the origin/development
of life?

accepted.question_text: Are there non-iterative physical mechanisms, other than generate-and-test evolution or growth and development, that can effectively explore the vast combinatorial state space of viable living forms—for example by quantum collapse to a viable candidate in a single step—or is an iterative process still required to prepare a state whose collapse has non-negligible probability of yielding a viable candidate?
accepted.context_brief: non-iterative search of biological possibility space

evidence.quote:
Are there non-iterative processes that can effectively explore a Vast state space
of possibilities?

Are there physical mechanisms other than generate and test or growth and development, that could
be exploited in order to explore the Vast state space of possibilities more effectively, and in a non-iterative
manner? Could, for example, some form of quantum collapse to a viable candidate be possible in a single
step? Or would there still need to be some iterative process to arrange the superposition state into a
form where collapse yields a viable candidate with non-negligible probability?
These are open questions.

accepted.question_text: Does the possibility of self-reference in a natural system require, imply, or use natural time, given that an act of self-reference changes the system and can be represented as a present system referring to a future self rather than as a timeless circle?

evidence.quote:
Does the possibility of self-reference in a system require or imply the existence
or use of natural time?
Let us first focus on ‘natural’ systems. If we consider a natural system that refers to itself, how can
potential paradoxes of self-reference be avoided?

Hence a reference made by a present system to itself is resolved by a future self, which unwinds the
circle of the logical paradox into a natural time spiral, hence removing a potential paradox.

accepted.question_text: Are there cases in mathematics or science where the time-dependent process that generates a result cannot be projected away from the result itself, so that one cannot separate the process of generating the result from the resulting formal object or scientific claim?

evidence.quote:
We are accustomed to think that a proof of a mathematical statement is timeless. But indeed, while
the proof looks timeless, it is not: A proof is an operational procedure that starts from assumptions,
applies inferences stepwise and ends in the production of a result. The result is a timeless formal object,
a tree of inferences, whose time-dependence can be projected away, but which would not come about
without the time-dependent operations of creating it.
Are there cases where this operation of projection cannot be executed? That is, are there cases where
one cannot separate the process aspect of generating the result from the result itself? Following Gödel’s
incompleteness theorem, is this what Mathematics is? More generally, is Science in a similar position?

accepted.question_text: For a self-referential Liar Paradox sentence treated as a temporal oscillator that alternates between truth values through natural time, what determines the oscillator’s rate of time, and how is that rate related to the frame rate of the cognitive system observing and calculating the sentence’s truth value?

evidence.quote:
Grim started with the basic Liar Paradox (“This
sentence is false”) and pointed out that it is a paradox only if one insists on a single constant (i.e., time-
less) truth value. If one places this self-referential sentence in what we call natural time, unwinding the
circle into a helix as in figure 2, then it can be seen to encode a simple oscillator that bounces between
TRUE and FALSE through time.

One interesting question here is the rate of time: how fast does the Liar Paradox oscillate? It is
relative, to the frame rate of whatever cognitive system is observing it and calculating the truth value.
This is another kind of time that is set by the cognitive system and its interaction with the world.

accepted.question_text: What dynamics are necessary and sufficient for a living system to creatively interpret physical memory structures—such as behavioral engrams or genomic sequences—in a way that supports forward-looking goals, especially when memory and self persist through radical bodily or neural remodeling such as metamorphosis or regeneration?

evidence.quote:
The flow of information within this architecture is fascinating and enables behavioral robustness that
we have yet to even begin to emulate in silico [62, 63]. The caterpillar can be trained, and the butterfly
or moth will retain those memories, despite the fact that the brain, the conventional view of the site
of memories, is almost totally destroyed and rebuilt during the metamorphosis process [64], and the
fact that those memories have to be decoded in the context of a totally different body structure and
behavioral repertoire

Crucially in biology, memories (whether behavioral engrams or genomic sequences) must be
interpreted: a dynamic that eventually scales cell-level problem-solving into the advanced intelligence we
observe in brainy animals [65]. The precise dynamics necessary and sufficient for creative interpretation
of physical memory structures in a way that facilitates forward-looking dynamic goals remains very
poorly understood, but it is clear that electrophysiology of all cells, not just of nerves and muscle, is
centrally involved.

accepted.question_text: What mathematical formalisms and computational tools can model a self-modifying open system that changes its own rules and remains open to its environment, especially when open-endedness requires models and metamodels that can produce level-1 innovations and level-2 transformations rather than only level-0 state variations?

evidence.quote:
Banzhaf et al. [13] consider variation to be a normal property of any dynamical system, and so not the
kind of novelty of interest in open ended systems. So they define an open ended system to be one that
continually produces type-1 and type-2 novelties.

This suggests the route to modelling open ended
self-modifying systems, including living systems, is to use models and languages that themselves have
self-modifying capabilities

What are appropriate mathematical formalisms and computational tools for mod-
elling a self-modifying system that changes its own rules, and is open to its en-
vironment?

accepted.question_text: What computational tools and modeling paradigms can implement and run simulations of self-modifying open systems whose programs, operators, structures, rules, or representational categories can evolve rather than remain fixed?

evidence.quote:
What are effective tools and modelling paradigms for implementing and running
(simulations of) self-modifying open systems?

Self-referential systems are natural in computing; self-modifying ones less so, but not unknown. Com-
puter science gives us tools for modelling, simulating, and analysing such systems; a few approaches are
summarised here.

accepted.question_text: How can a dynamic programming language or metamodel be used to generate dynamic models or programs for open-ended systems, and how can a dynamic metalanguage be developed for generating dynamic languages that themselves support open-ended self-modification?

evidence.quote:
The Banzhaf et al. [13] definition of openendedness requires that models and metamodels be dynamic, be
able to change as the system evolves in time (sec.55.5). However, conventional mathematical modelling
techniques and computer programming languages are static: they do not change, and they have no
facilities for their models to change, as the system evolves.

Developing a method for using such a
language (metamodel) to generate dynamic models (programs) of open ended systems remains an open
research topic; developing a dynamic metalanguage for generating dynamic languages even more so.

accepted.question_text: What analysis tools can interrogate self-modifying, evolving, open-ended systems once they move outside their current behavioral models and outside measures based on those models?

evidence.quote:
What are appropriate analysis tools for interrogating self-modifying, evolving,
open systems?
An open ended system will eventually move outside its current model of behavior, and hence outside any
measure based on that model [110]. This makes designing analysis tools challenging.

Analysis tools exist, for example, the MODES (‘Measurements of Open-
ended Dynamics in Evolving Systems’) toolbox [121], which has been applied to a range of self-modifying
systems, including ecologies and major evolutionary transitions.

accepted.question_text: How can rigorous mathematical sketches of self-referential biological organization, such as Rosen’s metabolism-repair systems interpreted through fixed points, domain theory, or coalgebras, be bridged to plausible biological mechanisms, and when should concurrent-process formalisms replace rigid sequential function application for modeling autopoiesis?

evidence.quote:
It is possible to find a λ-calculus term providing a uniform
solution to these equations, making use of the fixpoint (or ‘paradoxical’) combinator Y [122]. This in
turn can be interpreted mathematically in terms of domain theory. Related ways of interpreting ( M, R)
systems using coalgebras in the guise of non-well-founded sets are described in [123]. Thus we see some
lineaments of a rigorous theory underpinning Rosen’s ideas using the mathematics of self-reference. A
remaining challenge is to bridge the (large) gap between these mathematical sketches and plausible
biological mechanisms.

As those authors note, it may be more natural to use an approach based on
concurrent processes, rather than the more rigid and sequential notion of function application.

accepted.question_text: What mathematics can describe game-theoretic systems in which the number of players or selves changes in real time as a function of the players’ actions, such as biological tissues that can merge, split, or generate new individual decision-makers?
accepted.context_brief: game theory with changing numbers of selves

evidence.quote:
One approach that needs to be developed is game theory in which the number of players not only
changes, but changes as a function of the actions of the players.

Depending on what it does, 1 or 2 individuals will result, and the calculus of decision-making will
change because its actions not only change its rewards and what happens, but also change the number
of individuals that exist and make decisions.

To our knowledge,
the mathematics needed to understand the behavior of systems that are self-modifying in the sense of
adding or removing selves in real time does not yet exist.

accepted.question_text: How can rule-changing games be given concrete game-theoretic models and solution concepts when domain-theoretic approaches to games closed under rule change face unresolved obstructions, including powerdomain constructions that do not fully capture desired standard game-theoretic features?

evidence.quote:
This is a remarkable tour de force , which uses much of the machinery in domain theory developed
up to that point in building these intricate models of economic behaviour, in which self-reference and
self-modification are central. However, the limiting features of domain theory itself seem to have led to
unresolved obstructions to further progress. In particular, the non-set-theoretic nature of powerdomains
means that, in lifting standard solution concepts from game theory to the domain theoretic setting, the
desired features are not fully captured.
Once again, as in the case of the biological modelling, a gap remains between the mathematical theory
and the concrete models one wishes to capture.

accepted.question_text: If representation is treated as a fundamental principle of living systems, how can representation be understood formally rather than merely invoked, and how does representation emerge from molecular-level phenomena where the distinction between a representation and the thing represented appears to disappear?
accepted.context_brief: representation as a fundamental biological principle

evidence.quote:
One candidate for such a principle is representation, with representation fundamental to living sys-
tems. But if we take representation as a fundamental principle, we need to understand it as such, rather
than simply invoke it as necessary or convenient. In biology this problem is likely to become one of
reductionism versus emergence as more phenomena come to be understood at the molecular level: at
the level of molecules, representation disappears; how does it emerge? This is another instance of the
coarse-graining problem mentioned previously.

It may be difficult to generalise representation in a formal way, since it covers such a wide range of
phenomena.

accepted.question_text: How useful is coalgebra for describing self-referential systems while they undergo structural evolution, given that coalgebra offers clarity for self-reference but may not handle evolving system structure adequately?

evidence.quote:
Coalgebra offers one promising approach to
dealing with systems characterised by self-reference. It has the advantage of providing the same clarity
and certainty offered by earlier mathematics. However, it is not clear how useful it will be in describing
systems as they undergo structural evolution.

accepted.question_text: What practical methods can model changes to the rules by which a system’s structure evolves, including higher-order evolutionary changes such as changes to the rules that generate structural change, so that biological and social-system transformations can be modeled hierarchically?

evidence.quote:
we still have no practical approaches to modelling changes to the rules by which the system structure
evolves, much less ways to model even higher level changes.

As already mentioned we currently
have no way of modelling higher order evolutionary changes, like changes to the rules that generate
structural change in the system. Without such hierarchical evolutionary modelling techniques it will be
impossible to model the transformations that characterise social systems.

accepted.question_text: How can an evolutionary model with multiple possible trajectories be calibrated and validated when there may be many fewer datasets than possible model outcomes, and when unobserved outcomes may either be possible-but-unrealized consequences of a structurally correct model or impossible artifacts of a structurally incorrect model?

evidence.quote:
For example, to use most models of real systems for prediction, they must
be calibrated. How do we calibrate an evolutionary model with multiple possible trajectories when we
may have many fewer data sets than the model has possible outcomes? If we calibrate so that the
model produces only observed outcomes, then if the model is structurally correct we will have seriously
mis-calibrated it, so that the model cannot predict outcomes that could have happened but did not; on
the other hand, perhaps the model is structurally incorrect, and those unobserved outcomes could not
in fact have happened. We have no way of knowing which of these possibilities is the case. This is a
problem that already arises in dynamical models with bifurcating trajectories [132] and at present there
is no known method for resolving it.
